Off the top of my head, roughly four years.
I have lived here since 2021, and I lived in the city for forty years.
It is far quieter and nowhere near as convenient.
I have been restoring it since 2021 and I have finished the kitchen.
There is a gruff old Italian cheese seller, and the market is fascinating.
I was sitting in gridlock when I snapped.
The plaster was removed by hand and the kitchen is being rewired.
We spoke a few weeks ago, and you had just moved. How is it going now?
Better than I expected. I have lived here since 2021, and it is far quieter than anywhere I lived before.
And the house? You said something about a kitchen.
I have been restoring it room by room. The kitchen is finished and it is being rewired at the moment. Sorry — let me backtrack. The kitchen is done. The wiring is not.
How long is that going to take, roughly?
Off the top of my head, two months. Come to think of it, everybody said two months about the roof as well, and that was a year ago.
Your English has changed since we last spoke. You know that, do you not?
To sum up eight weeks in one sentence: I still lose words, and now I keep talking. Looking back on it, that is the whole difference.
Bear with me, I am looking for the word in English.
Off the top of my head, roughly two months.
Sorry, let me backtrack. The kitchen is done, the wiring is not.
To sum up: I still lose words, and now I keep talking.
I do not sound native, and I hold my own in any meeting.

I have been speaking English at work for nineteen years and I have never once been mistaken for a native speaker. For a long time I thought that was the problem. Then a colleague from Lisbon said something to me that I still think about. She said, nobody in this room is grading your grammar. They are waiting to hear what you think. And she was right. In nineteen years, not one person has ever said to me, your English is not good enough. What they have said is, sorry, I did not follow that part. Which is a completely different problem, and a much easier one to fix. So my advice, off the top of my head, is this. Be concise. Stop when the point is made. And when you lose the word, do not stop talking. Go around it.

My teacher asked me to talk for three minutes about my own life, without notes, and I want to tell you what happened, because it was not what I expected. The first minute was terrible. I was translating in my head and I was long-winded and I said the same thing three times. Somewhere in the second minute something changed. I stopped listening to myself. I was just talking, and I was making mistakes, and it did not matter, because she was following me. Come to think of it, that was the first conversation in English where I forgot that it was English. The third minute went by and I did not notice. When she stopped me, I had said more than I say in most meetings. Looking back on it, that exercise was the milestone. Not a test I passed. A thing I stopped being afraid of.
